newsitem.title: USA: Chinese defense minister meets Clinton, Perry.
newsitem.headline: Chinese defense minister meets Clinton, Perry.

text.p: Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian met President Bill Clinton and U.S. defence leaders in a fence-mending visit on Monday and accused news media of exaggerating reports of nuclear arms proliferation by China.

Chi met briefly with Clinton at the White House and was welcomed to the Pentagon by Defence Secretary William Perry at the start of a twice-postponed, two-week visit to improve relations between Washington and Beijing.

Clinton and China's President Jiang Zemin met last month at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Manila as the two countries moved to shore up ties strained by trade disputes and U.S. concern over Chinese nuclear sales.
Washington has charged that China sold nuclear and missile technology to Pakistan and perhaps Iran, which Washington accuses of backing terrorism.

"I think on some of such issues the media have blown the issue of proportion, have exaggerated the issue," Chi said in response to a question on arms transfers from reporters at the Defence Department after a welcoming ceremony.

"Some of the issues have been exaggerated and some of these issues simply do not exist," Chi said, adding that China had carefully guarded its technology exports under a Missile Technology Control Regime agreement with Washington.
But Perry said the controversy over arms transfers would be a key subject during the Pentagon visit, the first by a Chinese defence minister to the United States since 1988.

"Nothing is more important to security and stability, not only of the region but in the entire world, (than) that two great powers, China and the United States, work together in the spirit of cooperation to prevent any weapons of mass destruction or the materials for those weapons from being proliferated to other countries," said Perry.
Chi, leading a 20-member delegation of military and foreign ministry officials, will meet Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott at the the State Department on Tuesday.
"I am confident through the talks between me and Dr. Perry we will be able to usher in a new stage in the relations between our two militaries," Chi told reporters.
"In particular, we are discussing some programmes to promote the relations between the two militaries."

Perry visited China in October of 1994, but Chi's return visit was postponed twice this year after the United States accused China of trying to influence Taiwan's presidential elections with military manoeuvres off Taiwan.
Despite China's continued efforts to isolate Taiwan diplomatically around the world, the United States maintains its close economic and security ties with the island.

Taiwan's government spokesman, Su Chi, on a visit to Washington, told reporters on Monday that U.S. Chinese relations and U.S.-Taiwanese relations should be on "parallel tracks." He added: "All our hope is that the development on that track (China) should not interfere with the development on this track (with Taiwan)."
Beijing's Chi was the commander of China's armed forces when the government crushed the 1989 pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.

A White House spokeswoman characterised his meeting with Clinton as primarily a courtesy call. But Clinton press secretary Mike McCurry said beforehand that Clinton and Chi would talk about "the broad nature of the relationship which has been moving in a positive direction."
U.S. relations with China went into a long downward spiral after the Tiananmen crackdown, but Clinton and Jiang agreed at their November 17 meeting to end the official estrangement.

McCurry told reporters last Friday that the United States did not consider the Tiananmen issue "irrelevant," but said Chi's visit was important because of the need to maintain peace and stability in Asia.
